segments.text: Right now, everyone seems to have an extremely firm opinion about where artificial intelligence
is taking us.
You usually hear from two main camps, the people who think it's going to solve all of
our problems, and the people who are convinced it's going to ruin everything.
But whether you're listening to an AI optimist or an AI warrior, they share one highly specific
trait.
They are absolutely certain they know exactly what's going to happen.
If you look back at history, human confidence in forecasting the future has a pretty terrible
track record.
The most massive, world-altering outcomes are almost always the ones that absolutely nobody
saw coming.
To see how this blind spot actually works in practice, we have to look past modern technology
and go back to a strange but entirely true story about city rats.
In 1902, the city of Hanoi was rapidly expanding.
To modernize, officials built a brand new, extensive sewer system beneath the streets,
which they considered a major point of civic pride.
Unfortunately, nine miles of dark, protected underground pipes also provided a perfectly
undisturbed breeding ground.
The new sewers quickly flooded the city with thousands of rats.
The government devised a solution that made perfect logical sense.
They set up a bounty system.
If a citizen killed a rat and turned in its severed tail as proof, the city would pay
them a small cash reward.
Thousands of tales poured into government offices.
The payouts were huge.
The plan seemed like a total success.
Then, people started noticing something strange.
Perfectly healthy rats running around the city streets, completely missing their tails.
The citizens had figured out the basic math of the bounty system.
A rat can live a long, healthy life without a tail, and more importantly, it can keep making
more rat babies.
To the rat hunters, killing a rat meant a one-time payment.
But letting a clipped rat live meant a permanent recurring revenue stream.
Soon, enterprising locals stopped hunting altogether.
They moved out to the countryside and set up dedicated rat farms, purposefully breeding
generations of rats just to harvest their tails for cash.
The payment system operated exactly the way the government designed it.
But because of human behavior, a plan created entirely to eradicate the rat population actually
caused people to purposefully breed millions more.
That exact same pattern, a well-intentioned plan producing an entirely unpredicted outcome,
didn't stop in 1902.
It happens constantly with new technology and science, sometimes as a costly mistake and
sometimes as a welcome surprise.
This graphic highlights two modern examples.
SMS was built for brief administrative texts, but young people turned texting into an everyday
way to stay in touch.
Conversely, Australia imported cane toads to eat sugar cane beetles.
Instead, they poisoned native animals and rapidly multiplied into an uncontrollable invasive
species.
Whether you look at Hanoi rats, cell phones in your pocket, or toads in Australia, the
lesson is exactly the same.
Whenever humans introduce a massive new variable into a complex system, the most significant
outcomes are never part of the original plan.
Now, let's aim that historical track record directly at today's debate over artificial
intelligence.
We have incredibly smart people making confident claims about exactly how AI will shape our
economy, our jobs, and our lives.
These experts are analyzing the data in front of them with serious rigor.
But just like the city planners in 1902, they cannot account for how millions of individual
people will actually adapt to, exploit, or break the system once they get their hands
on it.
The most defining widespread impact AI is going to have over your lifetime, whether it's
incredibly positive or deeply problematic, is probably something nobody in any lab has
even thought of yet.
That level of uncertainty shouldn't make you panic.
Instead, it means you have to keep your eyes open to how the world is actually reacting
to these tools right now.
You do not need to predict the future perfectly.
You need to recognize uncertainty, watch what people actually do, and build skills that still
matter when the forecast changes.
Some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted, and that is the best reason
to stay curious.
